SCOTUS to hear Trump’s case banning asylum claims at US border
This is the latest case related to immigration that the Supreme Court will hear in its 2027 term.
On Friday, the Supreme Court announced that it will hear a case regarding the Trump administration’s move to bar asylum claims from illegal immigrants crossing the southern border.
This is the latest case related to immigration that the Supreme Court will hear in its 2027 term, alongside the removal of migrants to third countries and detaining illegal immigrants within the US without a bond hearing. Decisions are expected by early July at the latest, per CBS News.
Trump issued a proclamation on day one of his return to office, stating that there is an “invasion” at the southern border. He suspended the entry of migrants crossing the border illegally between ports of entry and barred them from seeking asylum that would allow them to remain in the US. The DHS issued guidance implementing the directive.
Three nonprofits and 13 people filed a class-action lawsuit in February of 2025, with a federal judge later finding the asylum restrictions unlawful. The Trump administration appealed, and a divided three-judge panel upheld the decision in April. The policy has remained in effect as court proceedings continue.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer has said that the policy is Trump’s “main tool” for stopping illegal crossings. Sauer wrote in court filings, “And as several high-ranking government officials have explained, if allowed to take effect, the order below threatens to open the floodgates to illegal entry, once again overwhelming the system and rendering the southern border vulnerable to the trafficking of drugs, weapons, and other contraband and enabling cartels to re-establish control.”

Trump’s asylum restrictions face legal test in US Supreme Court
- By Reuters -
- Nov 14, 2026
WASHINGTON – The US Supreme Court agreed on Friday to consider the legality of President Donald Trump’s restrictions on access to asylum at the US-Mexico border, a hardline immigration policy his administration has credited with helping reduce border crossings.
The justices took up Trump’s appeal of a lower court’s ruling that found he exceeded his authority by denying migrants caught entering the country illegally the chance to apply for asylum.
The court is expected to hear arguments in the case in the coming months and rule by the end of June.
Trump, who has described the influx of migrants as an invasion, announced the new curbs just hours into his second presidential term on January 20, 2025. His policy sweeps more broadly than similar curbs put in place by his predecessor, Democratic former President Joe Biden, who limited asylum eligibility at the southern border in a bid to reduce illegal crossings.
Trump’s asylum policy is one of a number of measures his administration has taken as part of his crackdown on immigration pursued since returning to office last year. Top officials have also sought to persuade other nations to join in a global campaign to roll back asylum protections in an effort to reshape the post-World War Two framework around humanitarian migration.
Under Trump’s policy, migrants caught crossing the southern border illegally are barred from pursuing asylum claims. The prohibition also applies to migrants who arrive at official border crossings and lack certain medical or criminal history information, a requirement that advocates say is often impossible to meet for people fleeing violence.
Trump’s proclamation announcing the asylum restrictions — and the fast-track deportation procedures they are meant to enable — said the policy would remain in effect until the Republican president determines that the “invasion at the southern border” has ended.
‘CREDIBLE FEAR’ INTERVIEWS
Immigrant rights groups filed a class-action lawsuit challenging the policy on behalf of would-be asylum seekers who say they were denied a “credible fear” interview by US immigration officials before facing deportation. Such interviews are meant to determine whether migrants seeking asylum would face persecution in their home country based on race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion.
A Washington, DC-based federal judge ruled in favor of the immigrant rights groups in July 2025. The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in April upheld the judge’s ruling but largely agreed to block the decision from taking effect to let the administration appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, has been largely deferential to Trump in his second presidential term in challenges to his immigration policies.
In June, the court handed Trump a victory by backing the federal government’s authority to turn away asylum seekers when officials deem US-Mexico border crossings too overburdened to handle additional claims.
In September, the court let the administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown. The justices are due to hear arguments over the legality of that policy on December 9.

Supreme Court to review Trump’s asylum ban at southern border
WASHINGTON - The Supreme Court agreed Friday to review President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a key part of his administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown.
What they're saying:
The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications illegal. It's the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court.
Federal law gives people the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.
RELATED: Trump admits immigration enforcement may have been too 'tough' in first interview since midterms
At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.
Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.
The other side:
But immigration attorneys at the American Civil Liberties Union and National Immigrant Justice Center counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.
They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to unilaterally "eviscerate" legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.
Big picture view:
The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, immigration attorneys argue.
The asylum ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.
RELATED: Deportations not meeting Trump's aggressive targets, report finds
What's next:
The justices are expected to hear the case in the coming months and hand down a decision by the end of June.
It's the third major immigration case the high court will hear this term. The justices will also decide whether people can be swiftly deported to countries other than their homelands and if immigrants can be detained indefinitely during deportation proceedings.
The justices decided another asylum case in favor of the administration earlier this year, clearing the way for the Trump administration to potentially revive a "metering" policy that has been used to turn back immigrants in years past.
The Source: Information in this story came from The Associated Press, including its reporting on the Supreme Court’s decision to review the asylum ban, lower court rulings and arguments from the Trump administration and immigrant advocacy groups. This story was reported from Los Angeles.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court to weigh in on Trump's asylum ban, one of his top initiatives
sources.text:
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court on Nov. 13 said it will review President Donald Trump’s asylum ban at the United States-Mexico border, adding yet another dispute over a Trump immigration policy to the list of cases the court is considering.
The administration says Trump's policy of not allowing immigrants to seek asylum if they cross the border illegally is the “most important and effective” piece of the president's efforts to secure the southern border, which is one of his top initiatives.
But a federal judge ruled last year that Trump lacked the “sweeping authority” he asserted.
An appeals court likewise said the president cannot enact a categorical ban on asylum requests for some applicants.
The Justice Department told the Supreme Court that presidents have inherent authority to secure the border and protect national security.
On his first day back in office, Trump issued a proclamation declaring crossings at the southern border an “invasion” and sought to prevent many immigrants arriving there from applying for asylum.
Immigrant rights groups and individual immigrants sued. They argue that Trump is eviscerating the protections Congress created for people fleeing persecution or torture.
Federal immigration law allows anyone in the country or at an official entry port to apply for asylum.
Processing an asylum request can take years, and many migrants have been allowed to remain in the United States in the meantime.
That’s created an incentive for migrants to come to the United States, the administration argues, even if they know their asylum claims will eventually be rejected.
The Justice Department says that because the decision of whether to grant asylum is up to the government, the president can also broadly decide that anyone who illegally crosses the border is not eligible for asylum.
That policy has dramatically reduced – by 93 percent − the number of migrants apprehended at the border, according to the government.
Immigrant rights groups challenging the policy responded that border apprehensions were already down more than 90 percent from their peak before the change took effect.
“If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border,” lawyers for the groups told the Supreme Court, “Congress must provide them.”
Other immigration cases the court will hear this term include challenges to two more practices important to the president’s crackdown on immigration.
The court will decide whether the administration can detain millions of immigrants without giving them a chance to seek bond, and whether it can deport immigrants to countries other than their own without letting them argue that they could be persecuted or tortured there.
Decisions are expected by the end of June.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Will Decide Whether Trump Can Shut Off Asylum at the Southern Border
sources.text:
Supreme Court Will Decide Whether Trump Can Shut Off Asylum at the Southern Border
The Supreme Court agreed Friday to decide whether President Donald Trump can bar migrants who cross the southern border illegally from seeking asylum, taking up one of the central pieces of his immigration crackdown.
The justices will review a federal appeals court ruling that found the policy unlawful, the Associated Press reported. The ban has stayed in effect while the case moved through the courts, and a ruling is due before the end of June, NBC News reported.
The case, Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, grows out of a proclamation Trump signed on Jan. 20, 2025, his first day back in office, declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border.”
The proclamation suspended the entry of migrants “engaged in the invasion,” and Homeland Security guidance that followed barred them from applying for asylum and allowed quick removal without some of the procedures in federal law, SCOTUSblog reported.
According to the court’s order, the justices will weigh two questions: whether the proclamation and its guidance are lawful, and whether federal immigration law bars the class-wide relief a district judge granted. They declined to take up a third question about the class definition.
The administration told the justices the border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security.”
The policy, Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” He pointed to a provision of immigration law that lets the president restrict the entry of anyone whose arrival would be “detrimental to the interests of the United States,” NBC News noted.
The challengers, 13 unnamed migrants who say they were persecuted or tortured at home and three immigrant advocacy groups represented by the American Civil Liberties Union, argue the ban flouts the asylum process Congress wrote into the Immigration and Nationality Act.
The president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute,” their lawyers wrote.
U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss sided with the challengers in July 2025. In April, a panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit largely upheld his ruling, with Judge J. Michelle Childs writing that Congress “did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts,” SCOTUSblog reported.
Judge Justin Walker dissented in part, arguing that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications. He agreed, however, that the government cannot send migrants to countries where they would be persecuted.
The D.C. Circuit kept its ruling on hold during the appeal, which has allowed the administration to keep the restrictions in place.
The asylum fight joins a growing list of Trump immigration cases on the court’s docket, including challenges to deportations to “third countries” and to holding immigrants without a hearing, the Washington Examiner reported. In June, the court blocked Trump’s order limiting birthright citizenship.

sources.news_title: US Supreme Court to review President Trump’s restrictions on asylum seekers at southern border
sources.text:
The US Supreme Court agreed Friday to review the legality of President Donald Trump’s restrictions on asylum seekers at the southern border, taking up questions about the president’s authority to block certain migrants from applying for protection and the scope of relief federal courts may grant in challenges to the policy.
In an order granting certiorari in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services (RAICES), the Court agreed to consider two questions: whether Presidential Proclamation 10888 and its implementing guidance are lawful, and whether 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1) bars the classwide relief ordered by the district court. The Court did not grant review of the government’s third question, which challenged the class definition under Article III of the Constitution and Rule 23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
President Trump issued Proclamation 10888, titled “Guaranteeing the States Protection Against Invasion,” on January 20, 2025. The proclamation suspends the entry of certain noncitizens crossing the southern border and restricts their access to statutory provisions that would allow them to remain in the United States, including the asylum process. It also imposes restrictions on people who fail to provide specified medical and criminal history information. The administration relies on provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act authorizing the president to suspend entry under certain circumstances.
The policy has been challenged by 13 individual plaintiffs and three nonprofit organizations, including RAICES, Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center, and the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project. They argue that the proclamation and its implementing guidance unlawfully bypass procedures and protections established by Congress. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1158, a noncitizen who is physically present in or arrives in the United States may generally apply for asylum regardless of immigration status or whether they arrive at a designated port of entry.
In April, the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed the district court’s ruling that the proclamation and guidance were unlawful insofar as they replaced statutory removal procedures with procedures not authorized by the Immigration and Nationality Act. The appeals court distinguished the president’s authority to suspend entry from the authority to remove people already in the United States, concluding that the statutory provisions cited by the administration did not authorize the president to create alternative removal procedures that displaced protections enacted by Congress.
The government also argues that Section 1252(f)(1) limits lower courts’ authority to issue classwide relief affecting the operation of certain provisions of the immigration laws. The D.C. Circuit rejected that argument, finding that the district court’s injunction did not restrain the operation of provisions covered by the statutory limitation. The Supreme Court’s review will address whether that interpretation was correct. The restrictions remain in effect while the litigation proceeds, as the lower court’s ruling has been stayed.

sources.news_title: US Supreme Court Takes Up Asylum Curbs
sources.text:
Mexico: US Immigration Law
Key Facts
—Order. On Friday, 13 November 2026, the US Supreme Court agreed to hear case No. 26-239.
—Scope. The Court took two questions: is the ban lawful, and may courts order class-wide relief.
—In force. The asylum restrictions stay in force while the case proceeds.
—Timing. No argument date is set, according to the Court’s docket.
—Border. People who cross from Mexico illegally cannot apply for asylum while the proclamation stands.
The US Supreme Court will decide whether a president can suspend asylum claims at the Mexican border by proclamation. Its order on Friday leaves the restrictions in force while the justices take the case.
Why It Matters
Since 20 January 2025, people who cross the border from Mexico illegally have been barred from applying for asylum under a presidential proclamation. On Friday, 13 November 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to test whether that bar is lawful.
US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the federal border agency, said on 16 October 2026 that Border Patrol recorded fewer than 99,000 southwest border apprehensions in fiscal 2026, which ended on 30 September. It calls that a 95% decline from the more than 1.8 million a year recorded under the previous administration.
What the Court Agreed to Decide
The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, No. 26-239, named for Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security Secretary. The Court’s docket shows it granted the government’s petition on 13 November 2026, limited to the first two of three questions.
Question 1 asks whether Proclamation 10888, titled “Guaranteeing the States Protection Against Invasion”, and its implementing guidance are lawful. Question 2 asks whether a federal law, 8 U.S.C.
1252(f)(1), bars the class-wide relief the district court ordered.
In Plain English
Asylum. US protection for people who fear persecution at home, which lets them stay and work.
Proclamation. A presidential order; this one, dated 20 January 2025, blocks asylum claims by people who cross the southern border illegally.
Class-wide relief. One court order that protects everyone in a defined group, not only the people who sued.
Solicitor General. The Justice Department lawyer who argues the federal government’s cases at the Supreme Court.
RAICES (the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services). One of three immigrant legal service providers that brought the lawsuit.
How the Case Got Here
Three immigrant legal service providers and 13 individuals sued over the proclamation in federal court in Washington. On 2 July 2025 the district court ruled for them in substantial part, held the asylum bar unlawful and certified a class of people subject to the proclamation.
On 1 August 2025 a panel of the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit paused the asylum part of that ruling while the appeal ran. On 24 April 2026 a different panel upheld the district court in a divided opinion, with Judge Walker dissenting in part.
The appeals court denied a rehearing by its full bench on 23 July 2026. The ruling is on hold, and the asylum restrictions have stayed in force during the litigation.
Two Sides of the Argument
The government, in a petition signed by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, argues that asylum is “a purely discretionary benefit” and that officials need not accept applications that would be denied. It also says the class-wide order violates federal law and that the class is too broad.
The government adds that border encounters fell 93% after the proclamation, to the lowest levels since the 1960s. It says the asylum limits are central to that result.
Lee Gelernt, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union, is counsel for the plaintiffs on their brief opposing review. In their filing opposing review, the plaintiffs said the appeals court applied a reading of the law that the executive branch itself held for decades.
A Separate Case on the Same Border
This is not the earlier case Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, No. 25-5, about “metering”, the practice of limiting how many people officers inspect each day at border crossings. The Court decided that case on 25 June 2026, after arguments on 24 March 2026.
It held that a person standing in Mexico has not “arrive[d] in the United States” under the asylum statute until he crosses the border. That ruling concerned people waiting at the line, while the new case concerns people who cross without permission.
What the Ban Means at the Mexican Border
Anyone who crosses from Mexico illegally still cannot apply for asylum today. The Court’s order does not change who is covered today.
The Court’s order does not address Mexico’s side of the border. We found no official count of migrants now waiting in Mexican border cities because of the proclamation.
What to Watch Next
Under the Court’s Rule 25, the government’s main brief is due 45 days after the grant, which falls on Monday, 28 December 2026 unless the Court extends it. The plaintiffs then have 30 days after that filing to respond.
The Court has not published an argument date for this case. Arguments are heard after the parties file their written briefs.
What Is Not Known
The docket gives no argument date. No Supreme Court ruling on the merits exists, and the justices’ views are unknown.
What It Means for You
If you follow US border policy, this case asks whether an entry-suspension power can end asylum claims at the southern border. The restrictions apply while the case is pending.
Our earlier report on asylum claims filed in Mexico covers the other side of the line, and our story on a Chilean father held in Utah after an asylum bid shows the process on the US side. More coverage is in our Mexico news section.
Frequently Asked Questions
What did the Supreme Court decide on 13 November 2026?
It agreed to hear the government’s appeal in No. 26-239 and limited review to two of the three questions raised. It has not ruled on the merits.
Is the asylum ban in force now?
Yes. The appeals court ruling is on hold, so the restrictions have stayed in place during the litigation.
When will the Court hear arguments?
No date is set on the Court’s docket. Arguments are heard after the parties file their briefs.
Who brought the case?
Three immigrant legal service providers and 13 individuals sued on behalf of a class of people covered by the proclamation. Lee Gelernt of the American Civil Liberties Union is their counsel on the brief.

US Supreme Court to decide on Trump ban on asylum claims at the border
A section of the U.S.-Mexico border wall near El Paso, Texas, on June 6, 2024. (Photo by Ariana Figueroa/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court Friday granted the Trump administration’s request to decide whether the federal government can ban asylum claims at the southern border.
One of President Donald Trump’s first proclamations he signed at the start of his second term was a ban on asylum claims at the southern border on the grounds that there was an “invasion,” which the administration argued was a condition that allowed the president to invoke a section of the law to suspend asylum claims.
A federal judge found the policy unlawful, but decided to allow it to remain while litigation pursued. An appeals court upheld the lower court’s decision.
The justices agreed to answer two questions, whether the proclamation that bans asylum is lawful and if a class action suit should be allowed. The case will be argued sometime during the coming months.
This is the third major immigration-related case the high court has agreed to hear this term. The justices also will decide whether the Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries to which they have no ties to and whether immigrants can be indefinitely detained.
The justices earlier this year allowed the Trump administration to use a policy known as “metering” which allows immigration officials to turn away migrants applying from asylum at the southern border.
The American Civil Liberties Union is representing the three immigration groups that brought the suit: the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.
“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”
A decision from the justices is likely next summer.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON (OSV News) — The U.S. Supreme Court said Nov. 13 it would take up a case regarding President Donald Trump’s executive order banning asylum claims at the southern border.
A federal judge previously ruled that the policy, enacted by Trump on the first day of his second term, was unlawful, but it has remained in effect amid ongoing litigation.
The Trump administration asked the high court to overturn the lower court ruling.
James Percival, general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said in a post on X, “The single most important factor in the President’s success at the border has been this executive order, which he signed on day one.”
“After successfully preserving this authority in lower courts for two years, we look forward to presenting our arguments to the Supreme Court,” he said.
The American Civil Liberties Union, alongside other organizations, challenged the policy on behalf of those barred from making asylum claims.
‘Courts are right to reject this unprecedented power’
“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”
Federal law grants the right to seek asylum to those who fear persecution in their countries of origin, but grants the executive branch the authority to decide whether those claims are granted. However, the Trump administration has argued it can deny asylum claims outright.
The Trump administration’s record at the Supreme Court on its hardline immigration policies is mixed. In a landmark ruling in June, it struck down Trump’s executive order limiting birthright citizenship, finding the order violated the 14th Amendment. The same month, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end a program temporarily shielding eligible Haitian and Syrian immigrants living in the U.S. from deportation.
Earlier this year, the Supreme Court also ruled on a separate but related policy, allowing the Trump administration to reimplement a policy of turning away asylum-seekers along the U.S.-Mexico border before they enter the country, known as “metering.”
Court taking up ‘weighty immigration authority, legality issues’
Ashley Feasley, the legal expert in residence at the Immigration Law and Policy Initiative at The Catholic University of America Columbus School of Law, told OSV News that in taking up the case, the Supreme Court “continues its run of taking up cases this session that have weighty immigration authority and legality issues.”
“The Court will be specifically looking at whether a Presidential Proclamation issued by President Trump in January 2025 can effectively prevent certain individuals from entering the country and claiming asylum and other lesser protections like withholding of removal,” Feasley said. “The outcome of this case will have large policy implications as it will likely shape the Trump Administration’s and future Administrations’ ability to operationalize access to asylum at U.S. borders.”
Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles: the right of persons to migrate in order to sustain their lives and those of their families; the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration; and a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.
The high court is expected to hear the case in spring 2027, with a decision by the end of its term, typically in June.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Takes Up Trump's Asylum Ban at the Border
sources.text:
The Supreme Court agreed Friday to decide whether President Donald Trump can suspend access to asylum at the southern border, taking up the administration's appeal of rulings that found his first-day proclamation unlawful. The case, Mullin v. RAICES, is expected to be argued in the spring of 2027, and a decision would come by the end of the court's term in June of that year. The administration has kept the policy in force while the litigation proceeds, so the justices' eventual ruling will be the final word on how far a president's power to keep noncitizens out reaches into the asylum system Congress created.
The dispute centers on a proclamation Trump issued on Jan. 20, 2025, declaring that "an invasion is ongoing at the southern border" and suspending the entry of noncitizens "engaged in the invasion," under a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act known as Section 212(f). The proclamation also indicated that those noncitizens could no longer seek protections such as asylum, and the Department of Homeland Security issued guidance to carry it out. Challengers say the order shuts off the asylum process for people who cross the border without authorization, including those who say they are fleeing persecution.
The challenge was filed on Feb. 3, 2025, by the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, known as RAICES, along with Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project. U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss in Washington certified a class of everyone who is or will be subject to the proclamation. He found that neither the Constitution nor federal immigration law gives the president authority to replace the rules and procedures Congress enacted for handling asylum claims, and he threw out the DHS guidance and barred officials from carrying it out under the proclamation. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit granted the administration a partial stay in 2025, allowing the policy to apply to asylum applications while keeping the ban on applying it to withholding of removal and to protection under the Convention Against Torture. The appeals court heard arguments on Nov. 3, 2025, and ruled in April 2026 that the proclamation is unlawful, then paused its own ruling pending Supreme Court review.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued in the administration's petition that the proclamation rests on a commonsense understanding of the president's inherent and delegated powers to exclude noncitizens. He said Trump acted within his authority in making clear in advance that asylum applications from people who violate the entry suspension would be denied, and in directing that the government need not accept what he called futile applications from them. The administration has continued to enforce the policy while the case moves forward.
The challengers reject that reading. Lee Gelernt, the ACLU lawyer who leads the case, said the president cannot unilaterally override the protections Congress gave people fleeing danger. The plaintiffs argue that the proclamation violates the asylum and withholding provisions of immigration law, the statutes that carry out the Convention Against Torture, and the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act. They also dispute the premise that there is an invasion at the border. Several of the individual plaintiffs say they fled political imprisonment, torture and threats from the Taliban, and the groups representing them say the administration has kept blocking access to asylum even after the lower courts ruled against it.
The legal question turns on how much Section 212(f) can carry. The provision lets a president suspend the entry of noncitizens he finds would be detrimental to the interests of the United States, and in 2018 the Supreme Court upheld Trump's travel ban 5-4 under that language. The asylum case asks something different: whether a suspension of entry can also eliminate the ability to apply for asylum, which federal law extends to people who reach U.S. territory whether or not they arrive at a designated port of entry. The administration says the president's powers over entry cover the situation, and the challengers say Congress already decided how asylum claims must be handled.
The court's decision is one of several immigration matters pending before the justices. On Sept. 29, in an unsigned order, the court cleared the administration to resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own while it prepares to decide whether the policy violates federal law and due process. On Thursday, a federal judge in Washington weighed whether to block the administration's latest birthright citizenship executive order and suggested that the government's reading of the Supreme Court's recent citizenship ruling is contradicted even by Justice Samuel Alito's dissent in that case.
The border has also been in the news this week for other reasons. On Thursday, Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico unless it stops a migrant caravan, and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said no caravan has reached the U.S. border since January 2025. The asylum case will not resolve that dispute, but it will determine what legal options migrants who do reach the border have once they arrive.
The timing adds a political layer. Republicans lost control of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and Democrats take over both chambers in January. The question before the justices is statutory, whether the immigration law that Congress wrote limits what a president can do by proclamation, but the case will be argued as the administration's immigration agenda faces a Congress that will oversee it. Neither the White House nor the Department of Homeland Security has commented publicly on the decision to take the case, according to the reports reviewed.
The dates on the record are specific. Trump issued the proclamation on Jan. 20, 2025, and the challenge was filed on Feb. 3, 2025. The D.C. Circuit heard arguments on Nov. 3, 2025, and ruled against the administration in April 2026. The Supreme Court granted review on Nov. 13, 2026, and it is expected to hear arguments in spring 2027 and decide by the end of June.

Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.
The Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s suspension of entry would be quickly removed without some of the procedural protections provided by law.
The challengers in the case are a group of 13 individuals who say that they have been persecuted or tortured in their home countries, as well as three immigration-related nonprofits. They sought to file a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Washington, arguing that both the proclamation and the guidance violate federal immigration law.
U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss recognized a class of challengers, made up of immigrants who are or would be subject to Trump’s proclamation. He concluded that the DHS guidance was unlawful and threw it out, and he barred DHS officials from implementing those actions under the proclamation.
A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit initially paused part of Moss’ order, but a different panel later largely upheld it on the merits. Judge J. Michelle Childs, joined by Judge Cornelia Pillard, wrote that the “text, structure, and history” of federal immigration law “make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts. The Proclamation and Guidance are thus unlawful to the extent that they circumvent … removal procedures and cast aside federal laws affording individuals the right to apply and be considered for asylum or withholding of removal protections,” a more limited form of protection from deportation.
Judge Justin Walker dissented in part. Although he contended that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications and therefore can dispense with the application process altogether on the ground that he would deny the applications, he agreed with the majority that the government “cannot remove aliens to countries where they will be persecuted, and the Proclamation and Guidance cannot strip them of mandatory procedures that protect against that removal.”
The D.C. Circuit agreed to keep its ruling on hold while the government appeals, allowing the government to maintain the asylum restrictions.
Contending that the U.S.-Mexico border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that “suspending the illegal entry of aliens and precluding their access to asylum” is “[t]he most important and effective pieces of the President’s response.”
Trump’s proclamation, Sauer continued, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” Therefore, he said, Trump “acted well within his authority in preemptively indicating that asylum applications filed by aliens who violate the proclamation’s entry suspension would be denied—and in effectuating that discretionary policy choice by directing that the government need not accept futile asylum applications from those aliens.”
Sauer also told the court that the lower courts did not have the power to apply their order to a whole class of challengers. Federal immigration law, he argued, expressly bars lower courts from issuing orders that require federal officials to enforce or implement specified provisions of federal immigration law –including those “allowing aliens to assert an asylum claim … and obtain a hearing before being subject to expedited removal.”
And in any event, Sauer continued, the class of challengers also violates the rules governing class actions because it “sweeps in aliens who are currently overseas and have no imminent plans to enter the United States (much less enter illegally).” Those noncitizens, he wrote, have not been injured and therefore cannot be part of the class; they “will become future class members here only if they choose to illegally enter the county.”
The challengers urged the justices to deny review, telling them that the D.C. Circuit’s ruling “correctly held that the President may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.” They also pushed back against the administration’s suggestion that the proclamation and guidance were intended to address an “unprecedented crisis,” countering that “the facts say otherwise. By January 2025, before the Proclamation took effect, border apprehensions had returned to historically routine levels, down over 90 percent from their peak. If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border, Congress must provide them.”
The statute on which Trump relies for the proclamation, the challengers continued, “does not speak to the removal of noncitizens who are already here. Nor does it authorize the Executive Branch to abrogate Congress’s protections against removing noncitizens to persecution or torture.” Instead, they wrote, federal immigration law “provides that noncitizens ‘may apply’ for asylum, ‘irrespective of … status’” or where and how they entered the United States. In conflict with “statutory command,” the challengers contended, “the Proclamation and Guidance dictate that statutorily eligible noncitizens may not apply for or receive asylum.”
The challengers also rejected the administration’s suggestion that the lower courts could not have broadly barred the Trump administration from implementing the proclamation and guidance. The law stripping the lower courts of the power “to enjoin or restrain the operation of” some federal immigration laws does not apply here, they said, because Trump’s proclamation relies on other laws that are not implicated by that bar.
The court agreed to consider the legality of Trump’s proclamation and the guidance, as well as Moss’ power to enter an order providing broad relief, but it turned down the government’s request to weigh in on whether the class violates the rules governing class actions.
The court also agreed to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha on Friday, involving whether a California-based financial-services company violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering in July 2021, although that data was not scheduled to be reported until August of that year. In a lawsuit brought by investors, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled against the company, prompting it to come to the Supreme Court in February.
The company asked the justices to decide two questions, involving the effect of the company’s failure to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider significant to their decisions on compliance with federal securities laws and regulations.
The investors asked the justices to stay out of the case, telling them that “[t]here is nothing radical … about the decision below,” much less anything worthy of the Supreme Court’s intervention. Although the company “disagree[s] with the outcome,” the investors said, it “do[es] not propose that this Court adopt legal rules in place of the existing standards.”
In a brief filed last month at the court’s request, the Trump administration agreed with Robinhood that the court should weigh in on the first question presented by the company’s petition for review. Sauer told the justices that the 9th Circuit’s ruling “threatens significant untoward consequences.”
The court on Friday agreed to decide one of the questions posed by Robinhood Markets’ petition: “[w]hether an issuer can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong” of the law at the center of the dispute “based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of” that provision, “without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.”
The justices will likely hear oral arguments in these cases sometime next spring.

WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court announced Friday it will rule on President Trump’s ban on asylum claims at the southern border, testing a key part of his hard-line policy on immigration.
At issue is a clash between the promise of asylum for those fleeing persecution and the reality of a border overwhelmed by hundreds of thousands who arrived seeking to apply.
Trump’s lawyers said his ban on asylum claims in January 2025 was his “single most effective policy” in ending the chaos along the border.
“Over preceding four years, at least eight million illegal aliens were encountered along the southern border,” Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer told the court, “and countless millions more evaded detection and illegally entered the United States.”
The Supreme Court sharply limited the right to asylum for migrants who say they are fleeing persecution.
The sheer numbers of people coming to the border had “overwhelmed the system,” making it impossible for U.S. officials to screen and interview asylum seekers, he said. Lacking facilities to detain applicants, most were released into the country.
But the American Civil Liberties Union and other immigration rights advocates said the right of individuals to seek asylum was recognized in U.S. law and could not be abolished.
The law authorizes asylum for people who can demonstrate they are fleeing persecution based on race, religion, nationality or belonging to a particular social or political group.
Federal judges in Washington agreed that asylum must be preserved. They said immigration officials were free to reject claims for asylum but they could not eliminate the right for the entire category of potential applicants.
However, their ruling was put on hold while the administration appealed to the Supreme Court.
“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”
A three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit found that immigration laws give people the right to apply for asylum at the border, and the president can’t circumvent that.
Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center, said the plaintiffs in the case “fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban. Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum.”
Instead, some of them “were removed to third countries and then pushed back to the very place they fled. This vicious attack on due process and human rights has put thousands of lives in danger.”
Federal immigration law gives the president broad authority to close the border to most migrants.
It says he “may by proclamation, and for such period as he shall deem necessary, suspend the entry of all aliens or any class of aliens as immigrants or nonimmigrants, or impose on the entry of aliens any restrictions he may deem to be appropriate.”
The court said it would hear the case of Mullin vs. Refugee and Immigrant Center early next year and rule by June.

The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on Friday to consider the legality of President Donald Trump’s restrictions on access to asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border, a hard line immigration policy his administration has credited with helping reduce border crossings.
The justices took up Trump’s appeal of a lower court’s ruling that found he exceeded his authority by denying migrants caught entering the country illegally the chance to apply for asylum.
The court is expected to hear arguments in the case in the coming months and rule by the end of June.
Trump, who has described the influx of migrants as an invasion, announced the new curbs just hours into his second presidential term on Jan. 20, 2025. His policy sweeps more broadly than similar curbs put in place by his predecessor, Democratic former president Joe Biden, who limited asylum eligibility at the southern border in a bid to reduce illegal crossings.

Top officials have also sought to persuade other nations to join in a global campaign to roll back asylum protections in an effort to reshape the post-Second World War framework around humanitarian migration.
Under Trump’s policy, migrants caught crossing the southern border illegally are barred from pursuing asylum claims. The prohibition also applies to migrants who arrive at official border crossings and lack certain medical or criminal history information, a requirement that advocates say is often impossible to meet for people fleeing violence.
Trump’s proclamation announcing the asylum restrictions – and the fast-track deportation procedures they are meant to enable – said the policy would remain in effect until the Republican president determines that the “invasion at the southern border” has ended.

Immigrant rights groups filed a class-action lawsuit challenging the policy on behalf of would-be asylum seekers who say they were denied a “credible fear” interview by U.S. immigration officials before facing deportation. SCOTUS to hear case on Trump asylum policy
sources.text:
The Supreme Court will consider President Donald Trump’s restrictions on asylum at the southern border.
The Trump administration asked the high court to overturn an appeals court ruling that found his executive order restricting asylum applications was illegal. The restriction has remained in place during the litigation.
The administration argues it can deny any asylum to migrants covered by the order and does not have to accept applications likely to be rejected.
A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia ruled that people have the right to apply for asylum at the border and the executive branch cannot prevent that.
Justices will likely hear the case in 2027 and issue a decision by the end of June.
The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, and was first brought in February 2025.
On the first day of his second term, President Donald Trump said the border surge was an invasion and added he was “suspending the physical entry” of migrants and their ability to seek asylum until he determined the emergency was over.
The American Civil Liberties Union and the National Immigrant Justice Center are representing immigrants in the case. They have contended in court filings that border crossings were falling before Trump took office in January 2025, and that his executive order would unlawfully “eviscerate” legal protections for people fleeing danger in their home countries.
At issue is federal law that allows migrants to seek asylum in the United States, while the executive branch decides who is granted asylum. The administration contends that, in certain countries, people need not fear persecution and an application for asylum would almost certainly be denied.
The Justice Department also argues that the processing time for applications can take years and has contributed to a large influx of immigrants at the southern border, according to The Associated Press.
Historically, asylum cases have been decided on a case-by-case basis. Immigration attorneys who sued to stop the order argue the law doesn’t allow a president to unilaterally halt asylum applications.
The high court will also hear cases about removing illegal immigrants to locations other than their origin country, as well as indefinite detention of illegal immigrants without access to a bond hearing.
This story is developing and will be updated.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court to review Trump’s asylum restrictions
sources.text:
The US Supreme Court has agreed to consider the legality of President Donald Trump’s restrictive asylum policies at the US-Mexico border.
Trump’s policy denies migrants caught entering the country illegally the opportunity to apply for asylum; the restrictions also affect migrants arriving legally but lacking required medical or criminal history information.
The big picture: The policy, announced hours into Trump’s second presidential term, is broader than similar actions by President Biden, further limiting asylum eligibility.
- Trump claims these measures help reduce illegal border crossings and describes the migrant influx as an “invasion.”
- Advocacy groups filed a class-action lawsuit, arguing that migrants were denied essential “credible fear” interviews by US immigration officials.
Flashback: A federal judge ruled against the policy in July 2025, and an appeals court upheld that ruling in April, but the decision was stayed pending Supreme Court review.
Go deeper: The Supreme Court, with a 6-3 conservative majority, has mostly supported Trump’s immigration measures since his return to office.
- Prior rulings this year allowed fast-track deportations and enabled the federal government to reject asylum claims when border capacity is overwhelmed.
- The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments over the asylum restrictions and issue a decision by the end of June.
- Trump’s administration is also encouraging other countries to participate in a global rollback of asylum protections, aiming to reshape international refugee policy.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court takes up Trump ban on asylum claims at US-Mexico border - The Catholic Telegraph
sources.text:
Supreme Court takes up Trump ban on asylum claims at US-Mexico border
WASHINGTON (OSV News) — The U.S. Supreme Court said Nov. 13 it would take up a case regarding President Donald Trump’s executive order banning asylum claims at the southern border.
A federal judge previously ruled that the policy, enacted by Trump on the first day of his second term, was unlawful, but it has remained in effect amid ongoing litigation.
The Trump administration asked the high court to overturn the lower court ruling.
James Percival, general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said in a post on X, “The single most important factor in the President’s success at the border has been this executive order, which he signed on day one.”
“After successfully preserving this authority in lower courts for two years, we look forward to presenting our arguments to the Supreme Court,” he said.
The American Civil Liberties Union, alongside other organizations, challenged the policy on behalf of those barred from making asylum claims.
‘Courts are right to reject this unprecedented power’
“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”
Federal law grants the right to seek asylum to those who fear persecution in their countries of origin, but grants the executive branch the authority to decide whether those claims are granted. However, the Trump administration has argued it can deny asylum claims outright.
The Trump administration’s record at the Supreme Court on its hardline immigration policies is mixed. In a landmark ruling in June, it struck down Trump’s executive order limiting birthright citizenship, finding the order violated the 14th Amendment. The same month, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end a program temporarily shielding eligible Haitian and Syrian immigrants living in the U.S. from deportation.
Earlier this year, the Supreme Court also ruled on a separate but related policy, allowing the Trump administration to reimplement a policy of turning away asylum-seekers along the U.S.-Mexico border before they enter the country, known as “metering.”
Court taking up ‘weighty immigration authority, legality issues’
Ashley Feasley, the legal expert in residence at the Immigration Law and Policy Initiative at The Catholic University of America Columbus School of Law, told OSV News that in taking up the case, the Supreme Court “continues its run of taking up cases this session that have weighty immigration authority and legality issues.”
“The Court will be specifically looking at whether a Presidential Proclamation issued by President Trump in January 2025 can effectively prevent certain individuals from entering the country and claiming asylum and other lesser protections like withholding of removal,” Feasley said. “The outcome of this case will have large policy implications as it will likely shape the Trump Administration’s and future Administrations’ ability to operationalize access to asylum at U.S. borders.”
Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles: the right of persons to migrate in order to sustain their lives and those of their families; the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration; and a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.
The high court is expected to hear the case in spring 2027, with a decision by the end of its term, typically in June.
Kate Scanlon is a national reporter for OSV News covering Washington. Follow her on X @kgscanlon.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Set to Hear Trump’s Ban on Asylum Claims at Border
sources.text:
The Supreme Court announced on Friday that it will review the legality of the Trump administration’s policy of categorically denying asylum claims from people crossing the southern border, taking up another major test of the president’s immigration agenda.
On President Trump’s first day back in office, he effectively shut down the ability of people fearing torture and persecution to apply for asylum protections at the border and then remain in the United States, declaring there was an “invasion” along the southern border. In a proclamation, he invoked what he called “the inherent right and duty of the executive branch to defend our national sovereignty.”
Immigration rights group quickly challenged the proclamation, and lower courts have found it to be illegal. But it has still largely been in force under a temporary court order. The Supreme Court case is expected to be the culmination of years of litigation over the ability of the government to prohibit migrants from claiming asylum at the border.
This Supreme Court term, which began in October and will conclude next summer, is shaping up to be dominated by Mr. Trump’s aggressive immigration policies. In December, the court will review the administration’s efforts to deport immigrants to so-called third countries where they have no ties, including nations that have faced allegations of human rights abuses. Next year, the court will consider the administration’s policy of indefinitely detaining immigrants who crossed the border illegally years ago.
In the asylum case the justices accepted on Friday, a central question is whether the president can override immigration law set by Congress. During the first Trump administration, officials struggled to come up with restrictive asylum policies at the border that would survive judicial scrutiny.
In his second term, the president adopted the prohibition on asylum claims at the border and has been fighting over the policy in court. D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, told the justices in court filings that their intervention was “urgently warranted” in part because the policy was Mr. Trump’s “main tool for stemming an unprecedented crisis of uncontrolled illegal entry.”
Mr. Trump’s initial proclamation was followed by guidance from the Department of Homeland Security that blocked people from applying for asylum who had crossed illegally.
As a result, the number of people crossing the southern border illegally has dropped to levels not seen in decades. Border Patrol agents made just over 6,000 arrests in June 2025, for instance, according to figures from the Department of Homeland Security. During the height of such crossings during the Biden administration, more than 200,000 people crossed in December 2023.
The immigrant rights groups brought the initial legal challenge on behalf of more than a dozen people who had been detained or removed from the United States without their asylum claims being addressed.
Many of those people had experienced political persecution in their home countries of Afghanistan, Cuba, Egypt, Peru and Turkey, according to court filings. Their lawyers said some were subjected to “traditional torture” at the hands of those governments.
“For nearly two years, the Trump administration’s unlawful asylum shutdown has deprived people seeking safety of their rights, placing vulnerable families, children and adults in harm’s way,” Melissa Crow, the director of litigation at the Center for Gender and Refugee Studies, said in a statement on Friday after the court had accepted the case.
She urged the justices to follow the lead of lower courts and find that the president “cannot unilaterally rewrite our immigration laws and defy the will of Congress to get its way.”
In July 2025, Judge Randolph D. Moss of Federal District Court for the District of Columbia ruled against the Trump administration’s asylum policy, finding that the Constitution and federal immigration law did not give Mr. Trump the expansive authority he claimed.
A divided appeals court panel in April largely upheld Judge Moss’s decision and rejected the administration’s view that it could “unilaterally and heedlessly return individuals even to countries where they will most certainly face persecution.”
The 2-to-1 decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia said Mr. Trump had to follow requirements outlined in the Immigration and Nationality Act and could not categorically deny asylum claims from people crossing from Mexico into the United States.
Zach Montague and Matt Schwartz contributed reporting.

“Over the last 4 years, the prior administration invited, administered, and oversaw an unprecedented flood of illegal immigration into the United States. Millions of illegal aliens crossed our borders or were permitted to fly directly into the United States on commercial flights and allowed to settle in American communities, in violation of longstanding Federal laws,” the president wrote in a proclamation.
“Many of these aliens unlawfully within the United States present significant threats to national security and public safety, committing vile and heinous acts against innocent Americans,” the president said.
“Others are engaged in hostile activities, including espionage, economic espionage, and preparations for terror-related activities. Many have abused the generosity of the American people, and their presence in the United States has cost taxpayers billions of dollars at the Federal, State, and local levels,” Trump said.
DOJ Solicitor General John Sauer told the Supreme Court that the president has the authority to bar aliens from entry to the US.
